passage:
Anirban stared at his phone as it buzzed a third time. Ma, calling from Dubai. Again he let it ring out. Dida looked up from her crossword but said nothing.
Next day at school his friend Sumit found him kicking a stone. "You skipped cricket. What happened?"
"Ma calls every Sunday and I have nothing to say. I know she went for my fees. But the house is quiet, and I'm angry, and I hate being angry."
Sumit shrugged. "Tell her that."
That Sunday Anirban called first. "Ma, I miss you. Some days I'm cross with you too."
A long pause, then a shaky laugh. "Tell me everything," she said. "I want the cross days as well."

qa.q: From which city was Ma calling Anirban?
qa.a: Ma was calling from Dubai.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he let the phone ring out?
qa.a: He felt a mix of missing his mother and being angry at the empty house, even though he knew she went to earn for his fees.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make that Sunday, and why did it help?
qa.a: He called first and told his mother he missed her and was sometimes cross, so the anger was spoken instead of turning into silence and resentment.

qa.q: How might Ma have felt when Anirban said he was sometimes cross with her?
qa.a: She was probably hurt but relieved, since she paused, laughed shakily and asked to hear the cross days too.

grounding: A teenager left with a grandparent misses a parent working abroad, and honest talk stops loneliness turning into resentment.

passage:
"Rekha, your mother is on video, come!" called Nani from the kitchen.
"One minute."
"You look tired, Rekha," said Preeti's voice through the speaker. "Did the exams go badly?"
"No, they went fine." Rekha stared at the table. "You missed prize day. Again. I know it's for my college fund. But I still wish you were in the second row."
"I wish it too, more than you know."
"Sometimes I'm angry, and then I feel bad about it."
"Don't feel bad. Be angry and tell me. I'd rather hear it than have you go quiet."
"Can you call on Friday nights, at a fixed time, even if it's only ten minutes?"
"Every Friday. And Nani can hold the phone so you can show me your prize."
Nani called from the doorway, "The certificate is already on the fridge."

qa.q: What did Rekha wish about prize day?
qa.a: She wished her mother had been in the second row.

qa.q: What is Rekha feeling as she talks about her mother missing prize day?
qa.a: She feels sad and a little angry, and guilty about being angry, because she knows the money is for her college fund.

qa.q: What did Rekha ask for that could keep distance from turning into resentment?
qa.a: She asked for a call every Friday night at a fixed time, even for ten minutes, which gives them a steady connection.

qa.q: How does Preeti see Rekha's anger?
qa.a: Preeti welcomes it, saying she would rather hear it than have Rekha go quiet, and she shares the wish to have been at prize day.

grounding: A teenager staying with a grandmother while a parent works in another place says she misses her and agrees regular calls.

passage:
In a small town in Oaxaca, Alejandro, fifteen, lived with his grandparents while his mother worked in a restaurant kitchen in Los Angeles. She'd left when he was nine.
Every Sunday she video-called. Lately he'd been answering in one-word sentences. "You're angry," his grandmother said. "I'm not," he said, and slammed the door.
At school, Soo-ah, whose father worked in Seoul, found him behind the gym. "My dad missed my birthday again," she said. "Sometimes I hate him for leaving. Then I feel terrible, because I know why he did."
Alejandro looked at her. "Same."
That Sunday, instead of one word, he told his mother, "I miss you. And I'm angry, a little." She was quiet, then said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm angry at the distance too." They talked for an hour. His grandmother made them both laugh at the end.

qa.q: Where does Alejandro's mother work?
qa.a: She works in a restaurant kitchen in Los Angeles.

qa.q: What was Alejandro feeling when he answered in one-word sentences?
qa.a: Alejandro felt lonely and resentful, angry at his mother's absence even though he knew why she left.

qa.q: What helped stop his loneliness turning into lasting resentment?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Soo-ah and then telling his mother the truth, that he missed her and felt angry, opened a real conversation.

qa.q: How might Alejandro's mother feel when he says he's angry?
qa.a: She likely feels sad but grateful for his honesty, since she says she is angry at the distance too.

grounding: Outside India, a teenager left with grandparents while a parent works abroad misses her, and honest talk keeps loneliness from becoming resentment.

passage:
At the parent-teacher meeting, every other student sat with a mother or father. Siddharth, fourteen, sat beside his grandfather, Shankar, whose hearing aid whistled every time the teacher spoke. His parents were both working in Dubai.
The teacher said Siddharth's marks had dropped and he'd stopped handing in homework. Shankar Thatha looked at Siddharth. "Why didn't you tell me?"
Siddharth stared at the table. "You wouldn't understand. And Amma and Appa only call to ask about marks."
Thatha was quiet. The teacher suggested the school counsellor, and a weekly call where Siddharth could talk about anything except marks.
That evening, Thatha called Dubai himself. "Talk to the boy about his cricket, his friends, anything. He misses you."
The next Sunday, Appa asked about cricket first. Siddharth talked for twenty minutes.

qa.q: Where were Siddharth's parents working?
qa.a: His parents were both working in Dubai.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when he said his parents only call to ask about marks?
qa.a: Siddharth felt lonely and resentful, missing his parents and hurt that they seemed to care only about marks.

qa.q: What steps helped Siddharth?
qa.a: The teacher suggested the counsellor and a weekly no-marks call, and Thatha told the parents that Siddharth missed them, which led to a real conversation.

qa.q: How might Thatha feel sitting at the meeting with his grandson?
qa.a: Thatha may feel worried and a little helpless, sad that Siddharth didn't tell him about his troubles.

grounding: At a school meeting, a teenager living with his grandfather while his parents work abroad reveals his loneliness, and honest talk and regular calls help.

passage:
Dear Papa,
Dhruv says I should write this instead of saying it on the phone, because I always go quiet on calls.
It's been two years since you went to Muscat. I know why. I know the house loan and Dhruv's school fees. I'm not a kid; I understand. But I'm sixteen and I've had to learn to shave from a video. Dhruv is ten and he asks Dadi when you'll come back every single night.
Dadi and Dada are good to us. But sometimes I'm angry and I don't know where to put it. Then I feel guilty, because you're working so hard for us.
Can we talk every Sunday, even for ten minutes? Not about marks or money. About anything.
Your son,
Kamal

qa.q: How long has Papa been in Muscat?
qa.a: It's been two years since Papa went to Muscat.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Kamal describe?
qa.a: Kamal feels angry and lonely, then guilty for feeling that way, because Papa is working so hard for the family.

qa.q: Why is Kamal's request for Sunday calls a good one?
qa.a: Regular calls about anything except marks or money can keep them close and stop Kamal's loneliness from hardening into resentment.

qa.q: How might Dhruv be experiencing Papa's absence?
qa.a: Dhruv, at ten, seems to miss Papa a lot, asking Dadi every night when he will come back.

grounding: A teenager living with grandparents while his father works abroad writes honestly about missing him, asking for regular calls to keep loneliness from becoming resentment.

passage: You asked how it is, living with Aaji and Ajoba. I'm Santosh, and it's been three years since Papa went to work in Muscat. I know why he went. The loan on the house, my sister's college. I know. But on my birthday last year he called four hours late, and I didn't pick up. I told my friend Harish I didn't care. That wasn't true. Ajoba found me on the terrace that night and didn't lecture. He said, "Tell your father what you told the terrace." So on Sunday I did. Papa went quiet, then said he misses my voice more than anything over there. Now we have a fixed call, Sunday, nine o'clock, and he tells me the boring parts of his week too. It still hurts sometimes. It just doesn't feel like anger any more.

qa.q: When is the fixed call with Papa?
qa.a: The fixed call is on Sunday, at nine o'clock.

qa.q: Why didn't Santosh pick up the late birthday call?
qa.a: Santosh was hurt and angry that Papa called four hours late, even while understanding why Papa works away.

qa.q: What made the difference between loneliness and resentment here?
qa.a: Talking honestly with Papa, nudged by Ajoba, and setting a regular Sunday call turned silent hurt into steady contact.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when Santosh finally spoke honestly?
qa.a: Papa likely felt sad and moved, going quiet and then saying he misses Santosh's voice more than anything over there.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager living with grandparents while a parent works abroad, whose loneliness is kept from turning into resentment by honest talk and regular calls.
